facts.claim: Gilbert and Lynch (2002) proved that when the network can lose messages, no read/write data store can guarantee both availability and atomic consistency: the CAP theorem.
In Gilbert and Lynch’s proof, available means every request that reaches a working server must get an answer.
Gilbert and Lynch model a partition as a network allowed to lose any number of messages; across a partition, every message is lost.
Amazon’s Dynamo paper (2007): a read must reach at least R of the N copies and a write at least W; when R + W is more than N, every read overlaps every write.
The Dynamo paper reports that the common (N, R, W) setting across several of its instances was (3, 2, 2).
Dynamo was built to be “always writeable”: for Amazon, rejecting a customer’s update, such as a shopping cart change, was a poor experience.
The Dynamo paper notes that raising W may increase the chance of rejecting requests, since more storage hosts must be alive to take a write.
In the Dynamo paper, “last write wins” means that when versions diverge, the one with the largest timestamp is kept as the correct version.
Dynamo describes itself as an eventually consistent data store: all updates reach all replicas eventually.
Jepsen: linearizability, one of the strongest promises a database can make, cannot stay available through a network break; some or all servers must stop answering.
Jepsen: read your writes means a client’s later reads show its own earlier write; that can keep working through a network break only if each client keeps talking to the same server.
Raft (Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014) keeps copies in step by electing one server as leader: every change goes through it, and it copies each change to the others.
Amazon’s Aurora docs (checked 2026-10-30): a copy in the same cluster usually trails a write by much less than 100 milliseconds, and by more when writes are heavy.
Over 24 hours of Amazon’s shopping cart, the Dynamo paper (2007) found 99.94% of requests saw exactly one version; clashing versions came mostly from many writers at once, not failures.
The Dynamo paper (2007) calls this its main advantage: each service sets its own N, R and W for the speed, uptime and safety of data it needs.
